claim: P4 ATPases use ATP hydrolysis to transport large lipid substrates across lipid bilayers.
source: The P4 ATPases use ATP hydrolysis to transport large lipid substrates across lipid bilayers.
evidence: This is a fundamental statement about P4 ATPase function presented in the abstract, supported by the broader scientific literature on these enzymes.

claim: Structures of the endosome- and Golgi-localized phosphatidylserine flippases such as yeast Drs2 and human ATP8A1 have recently been reported.
source: The structures of the endosome- and Golgi-localized phosphatidylserine flippases—such as the yeast Drs2 and human ATP8A1—have recently been reported.
evidence: This statement references prior structural studies, implicitly citing previous work.

claim: A substrate-binding site on the cytosolic side has not been found in previously reported P4 ATPase structures.
source: However, a substrate-binding site on the cytosolic side has not been found, and the transport mechanisms of P4 ATPases with other substrates are unknown.
evidence: This identifies a gap in prior knowledge that the current study addresses.

claim: The transport mechanisms of P4 ATPases with substrates other than phosphatidylserine are unknown.
source: However, a substrate-binding site on the cytosolic side has not been found, and the transport mechanisms of P4 ATPases with other substrates are unknown.
evidence: This statement identifies a knowledge gap addressed by the current study.

claim: Structures of S. cerevisiae Dnf1–Lem3 and Dnf2–Lem3 complexes were determined.
source: Here, we report structures of the S. cerevisiae Dnf1–Lem3 and Dnf2–Lem3 complexes.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by cryo-EM data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Substrate phosphatidylcholine molecules were captured on both the exoplasmic and cytosolic sides of Dnf1–Lem3 and Dnf2–Lem3.
source: We captured substrate phosphatidylcholine molecules on both the exoplasmic and cytosolic sides and found that they have similar structures.
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM density maps and structural models showing phospholipid molecules at both membrane sides.

claim: Phosphatidylcholine molecules on the exoplasmic and cytosolic sides have similar structures.
source: We captured substrate phosphatidylcholine molecules on both the exoplasmic and cytosolic sides and found that they have similar structures.
evidence: This is based on structural comparison of the bound lipids in the cryo-EM structures.

claim: Lem3 contributes to substrate binding.
source: Unexpectedly, Lem3 contributes to substrate binding.
evidence: This is supported by structural data showing Lem3 residues interacting with substrate and functional assays of Lem3 mutants.

claim: The conformational transitions of phosphatidylcholine transporters match those of phosphatidylserine transporters.
source: The conformational transitions of these phosphatidylcholine transporters match those of the phosphatidylserine transporters, suggesting a conserved mechanism among P4 ATPases.
evidence: This is based on structural comparison between the current structures and previously reported PS flippase structures.

claim: A conserved mechanism exists among P4 ATPases.
source: The conformational transitions of these phosphatidylcholine transporters match those of the phosphatidylserine transporters, suggesting a conserved mechanism among P4 ATPases.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural similarities observed between different P4 ATPase subfamilies.

claim: Dnf1/Dnf2 have a unique P domain helix-turn-helix insertion that is important for function.
source: Dnf1/Dnf2 have a unique P domain helix-turn-helix insertion that is important for function.
evidence: This is supported by structural identification of the motif and functional assays showing deletion of this motif strongly decreases transport activity.

claim: P4 ATPases may have retained an overall transport mechanism while evolving distinct features for different lipid substrates.
source: Therefore, P4 ATPases may have retained an overall transport mechanism while evolving distinct features for different lipid substrates.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combination of conserved structural features and unique elements observed in different P4 ATPase subfamilies.

claim: P-type ATPases are integral membrane proteins that mediate substrate transport across biological membranes by formation of ATP-dependent phosphorylated intermediates.
source: The large group of integral membrane proteins that mediate the transport of substrates across biological membranes by the formation of ATP-dependent phosphorylated intermediates are called P-type ATPases (Axelsen and Palmgren, 1998).
evidence: This is a well-established definition in the field, supported by citation.

claim: P-type ATPases are widely expressed in prokaryotes, archaea, and eukaryotes.
source: They are widely expressed in prokaryotes, archaea, and eukaryotes, and they play essential roles in many cellular processes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the distribution of P-type ATPases.

claim: P-type ATPases are phylogenetically divided into five subclasses (P1-P5).
source: P-type ATPases are phylogenetically divided into five subclasses (P1-P5), each have unique sequence motifs and transport different substrates (Bublitz et al., 2011; Palmgren and Axelsen, 1998).
evidence: This classification is supported by cited references.

claim: Each P-type ATPase subclass has unique sequence motifs and transports different substrates.
source: P-type ATPases are phylogenetically divided into five subclasses (P1-P5), each have unique sequence motifs and transport different substrates (Bublitz et al., 2011; Palmgren and Axelsen, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature on P-type ATPase classification.

claim: Most P4 ATPases function as a heterodimeric complex consisting of a catalytic α-subunit and a regulatory β-subunit.
source: Most P4 ATPases function as a heterodimeric complex: a catalytic α-subunit containing 10 transmembrane α-helices (TMHs) and a regulatory β-subunit of the Cdc50 (cell division cycle 50) protein family containing two TMHs.
evidence: This is established knowledge about P4 ATPase architecture.

claim: The catalytic α-subunit of P4 ATPases contains 10 transmembrane α-helices.
source: Most P4 ATPases function as a heterodimeric complex: a catalytic α-subunit containing 10 transmembrane α-helices (TMHs) and a regulatory β-subunit of the Cdc50 (cell division cycle 50) protein family containing two TMHs.
evidence: This is a structural characteristic confirmed by multiple P4 ATPase structures.

claim: The regulatory β-subunit of P4 ATPases belongs to the Cdc50 protein family and contains two transmembrane helices.
source: Most P4 ATPases function as a heterodimeric complex: a catalytic α-subunit containing 10 transmembrane α-helices (TMHs) and a regulatory β-subunit of the Cdc50 (cell division cycle 50) protein family containing two TMHs.
evidence: This is established knowledge about P4 ATPase β-subunit structure.

claim: The α-subunit of all P-type ATPases has a conserved architecture consisting of a transmembrane domain, an actuator domain, a nucleotide-binding domain, and a phosphorylation domain.
source: The α-subunit of all P-type ATPases has a conserved architecture consisting of a transmembrane domain (TMD), an actuator domain (A-domain), a nucleotide-binding domain (N domain), and a phosphorylation domain (P-domain) (Andersen et al., 2016; van der Mark et al., 2013).
evidence: This is well-established knowledge about P-type ATPase structure, supported by citations.

claim: The Post–Albers model proposes that substrate transport of P-type ATPases goes through a cyclic transition of E1–E1P–E2P–E2 states.
source: The 'Post–Albers' model proposed that the substrate transport of P-type ATPases goes through a cyclic transition of E1–E1P–E2P–E2 states (Post et al., 1972).
evidence: This is a well-known mechanistic model in the P-type ATPase field, supported by citation.

claim: The Post–Albers model is supported by structure and function studies of P2 ATPases.
source: This model is supported by the structure and function studies of the most well-understood P2 ATPases (Dyla et al., 2019; Toyoshima and Cornelius, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature on P2 ATPase mechanisms.

claim: P4 ATPases are involved in phospholipid translocation, flipping lipids from the extracellular or lumenal side to the cytosolic side.
source: P4 ATPases are involved in phospholipid translocation: they flip lipids from the extracellular side of the plasma membrane or from the lumenal side of internal organelles to the cytosolic side (Tang et al., 1996; Zhou and Graham, 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge about P4 ATPase function, supported by citations.

claim: P4 ATPases are important for creating and maintaining lipid compositional asymmetry in cell membranes.
source: They are important for creating and maintaining lipid compositional asymmetry in cell membranes.
evidence: This is a well-established biological role of P4 ATPases.

claim: The transport mechanism of P4 ATPases is substantially different from that of cation-transporting P-type ATPases because phospholipid substrates are large.
source: Because a phospholipid substrate is large, the transport mechanism of P4 ATPases is substantially different from that of the cation-transporting P-type ATPases, such as the sarcoplasmic reticulum Ca2+-ATPase (SERCA), the Na+/K+-ATPase, and the H+-ATPase.
evidence: This is inferred from the size difference between lipid and ion substrates and their respective transport mechanisms.

claim: There are five P4-ATPases in Saccharomyces cerevisiae: Drs2, Neo1, Dnf1, Dnf2 and Dnf3.
source: There are five P4-ATPases in Saccharomyces cerevisiae: Drs2, Neo1, Dnf1, Dnf2 and Dnf3, belonging to at least three distinct phylogenetic classes (Palmgren et al., 2019; van der Mark et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge about yeast P4 ATPases, supported by citations.

claim: The five yeast P4-ATPases belong to at least three distinct phylogenetic classes.
source: There are five P4-ATPases in Saccharomyces cerevisiae: Drs2, Neo1, Dnf1, Dnf2 and Dnf3, belonging to at least three distinct phylogenetic classes (Palmgren et al., 2019; van der Mark et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis cited in the references.

claim: Humans have 14 P4-ATPases.
source: Humans have 14 P4-ATPases (Andersen et al., 2016; Best et al., 2019; van der Mark et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by cited references.

claim: P4 ATPases have different tissue-specific expression, subcellular localization, and substrate specificity.
source: The P4 ATPases have different tissue-specific expression, subcellular localization, and substrate specificity.
evidence: This is general knowledge about P4 ATPase diversity.

claim: Yeast Drs2 transports phosphatidylserine and phosphatidylethanolamine in the trans-Golgi network and endosomes.
source: For example, yeast Drs2 transports phosphatidylserine (PS) and phosphatidylethanolamine (PE) in the trans-Golgi network (TGN) and endosomes (Natarajan et al., 2004; Zhou and Graham, 2009)
evidence: This is supported by cited functional studies of Drs2.

claim: Yeast Dnf1 and Dnf2 flip PE, phosphatidylcholine, and glucosylceramide in the plasma membrane.
source: while the yeast Dnf1 and Dnf2 flip PE, phosphatidylcholine (PC), and glucosylceramide (GlcCer) in the plasma membrane (Best et al., 2019; Pomorski et al., 2003; Roland et al., 2020; Roland et al., 2019; Stevens et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited functional studies.

claim: The first structural and mechanistic insights into P4 ATPases came from cryo-EM structures of S. cerevisiae Drs2–Cdc50 in auto-inhibited and active E2P states.
source: The first structural and mechanistic insights into the P4 ATPases came from recent cryo-EM structures of the S. cerevisiae flippase Drs2–Cdc50 in its auto-inhibited and active E2P states (Bai et al., 2019a; Timcenko et al., 2019)
evidence: This references prior structural studies with citations.

claim: Human ATP8A1–CDC50a structures were determined in six transport states (E1, E1-ATP, E1P-ADP, E1P, E2P, and E2Pi-PL).
source: and of its human homolog, ATP8A1–CDC50a, in six transport states (E1, E1-ATP, E1P-ADP, E1P, E2P, and E2Pi-PL) (Hiraizumi et al., 2019).
evidence: This references a prior structural study with citation.

claim: Drs2 and ATP8A1 belong to the same subfamily of P4 ATPases.
source: Drs2 and ATP8A1 belong to the same subfamily of P4 ATPases, and both transport the same substrates, PS and PE (Palmgren et al., 2019; Paterson et al., 2006; van der Mark et al., 2013; Zhou and Graham, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic classification and functional studies cited.

claim: Both Drs2 and ATP8A1 transport PS and PE.
source: Drs2 and ATP8A1 belong to the same subfamily of P4 ATPases, and both transport the same substrates, PS and PE (Palmgren et al., 2019; Paterson et al., 2006; van der Mark et al., 2013; Zhou and Graham, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by functional studies cited.

claim: Structural studies revealed an allosteric domain movement during lipid translocation in Drs2 and ATP8A1.
source: The structural studies revealed an allosteric domain movement during lipid translocation and identified a lipid-binding site at the exoplasmic side of membrane of this subfamily.
evidence: This is based on prior structural studies of these flippases.

claim: A lipid-binding site at the exoplasmic side of the membrane was identified in Drs2 and ATP8A1.
source: The structural studies revealed an allosteric domain movement during lipid translocation and identified a lipid-binding site at the exoplasmic side of membrane of this subfamily.
evidence: This is based on prior structural studies.

claim: Prior mutational studies identified amino acids in the exoplasmic lipid-binding site that are important for substrate recognition.
source: Prior mutational studies had identified amino acids in this exoplasmic lipid-binding site that are important for substrate recognition and had implicated a second substrate-binding site on the cytosolic side of the membrane (Baldridge and Graham, 2012; Baldridge et al., 2013; Baldridge et al., 2013; Roland et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by cited mutational studies.

claim: Prior studies implicated a second substrate-binding site on the cytosolic side of the membrane.
source: Prior mutational studies had identified amino acids in this exoplasmic lipid-binding site that are important for substrate recognition and had implicated a second substrate-binding site on the cytosolic side of the membrane (Baldridge and Graham, 2012; Baldridge et al., 2013; Baldridge et al., 2013; Roland et al., 2019).
evidence: This is based on cited mutational and functional studies.

claim: Dnf1 and Dnf2 share the same β-subunit, Lem3.
source: Dnf1 and Dnf2 share the same β-subunit, Lem3, and both are also capable of transporting PE and GlcCer (Jain et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge about these yeast flippases, supported by citation.

claim: Both Dnf1 and Dnf2 are capable of transporting PE and GlcCer.
source: Dnf1 and Dnf2 share the same β-subunit, Lem3, and both are also capable of transporting PE and GlcCer (Jain et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a cited functional study.

claim: Human homologs of Dnf1 and Dnf2, ATP10A and ATP10D, are implicated in diabetes, obesity, myocardial infarction, atherosclerosis, and Parkinson's disease.
source: Their human homologs, ATP10A and ATP10D, are implicated in diabetes, obesity, myocardial infarction, atherosclerosis, and Parkinson's disease (Folmer et al., 2009; BELNEU consortium et al., 2020; van der Mark et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies linking these proteins to disease.

claim: Cryo-EM structures of Dnf1–Lem3 were obtained in three different states: E1, E1P-ADP, and E2P.
source: Here, we report the cryo-EM structures of Dnf1–Lem3 in three different states (E1, E1P-ADP, and E2P)
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by cryo-EM data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Cryo-EM structures of Dnf2–Lem3 were obtained in five different states: E1, E1-ATP, E1P-ADP, E2P, and E2P-transition.
source: and Dnf2–Lem3 in five different states (E1, E1-ATP, E1P-ADP, E2P, and E2P-transition).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by cryo-EM data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Structure-guided mutagenesis and in vivo substrate-transport activity assays were performed.
source: We further performed structure-guided mutagenesis and in vivo substrate-transport activity assays.
evidence: This describes experimental methods used in the study.

claim: New phospholipid-binding sites at the cytoplasmic side were found in Dnf1–Lem3 and Dnf2–Lem3.
source: By comparing these PC flippase structures with the PS flippase structures previously reported, we found new phospholipid-binding sites at the cytoplasmic side and unique structural features during the ATP-dependent transport cycle in Dnf1–Lem3 and Dnf2–Lem3.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by structural data and comparison with prior structures.

claim: Unique structural features during the ATP-dependent transport cycle were found in Dnf1–Lem3 and Dnf2–Lem3.
source: By comparing these PC flippase structures with the PS flippase structures previously reported, we found new phospholipid-binding sites at the cytoplasmic side and unique structural features during the ATP-dependent transport cycle in Dnf1–Lem3 and Dnf2–Lem3.
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison and analysis of conformational states.

claim: Endogenous Dnf1–Lem3 and Dnf2–Lem3 complexes were purified from baker's yeast.
source: Endogenous Dnf1–Lem3 and Dnf2–Lem3 complexes were purified from baker's yeast using an anti-FLAG affinity column followed by size-exclusion chromatography
evidence: This describes the experimental purification method.

claim: Purified protein particles had detailed features in 2D averages of cryo-EM images.
source: and the protein particles had detailed features in the 2D averages of the cryo-EM images (Figure 1A–B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Materials and methods).
evidence: This is supported by the 2D class averages shown in the figures.

claim: DDM was used to solubilize the flippases.
source: We used the detergent dodecyl maltoside (DDM) to solubilize these flippases and lauryl maltose neopentyl glycol (LMNG) and cholesteryl hydrogen succinate (CHS) to stabilize the membrane protein complexes.
evidence: This describes the experimental method for protein solubilization.

claim: LMNG and CHS were used to stabilize the membrane protein complexes.
source: We used the detergent dodecyl maltoside (DDM) to solubilize these flippases and lauryl maltose neopentyl glycol (LMNG) and cholesteryl hydrogen succinate (CHS) to stabilize the membrane protein complexes.
evidence: This describes the experimental method for protein stabilization.

claim: ATPase activity of purified Dnf1–Lem3 and Dnf2–Lem3 was measured in the presence of GlcCer or sphingomyelin.
source: To ascertain the activity of the purified proteins, we measured the ATPase activity of both Dnf1–Lem3 and Dnf2–Lem3 in the presence of either a known substrate GlcCer or a non-substrate sphingomyelin at 0.1 mM concentration.
evidence: This describes the experimental assay performed.

claim: Only the substrate GlcCer but not the non-substrate sphingomyelin stimulated the ATPase activity of the enzymes.
source: We found only the substrate GlcCer but not the non-substrate SM stimulated the ATPase activity of the enzymes, and the stimulation is concentration dependent (Figure 1C–D).
evidence: This is supported by the ATPase activity assay data shown in Figure 1C-D.

claim: The stimulation of ATPase activity by GlcCer is concentration dependent.
source: We found only the substrate GlcCer but not the non-substrate SM stimulated the ATPase activity of the enzymes, and the stimulation is concentration dependent (Figure 1C–D).
evidence: This is supported by the dose-response data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Cryo-EM 3D maps of Dnf1–Lem3 in E1, E1P-ADP, and E2P states were obtained at resolutions of 2.8 Å to 4.0 Å.
source: We obtained cryo-EM 3D maps of the S. cerevisiae Dnf1–Lem3 in the E1, E1P-ADP, and E2P states and Dnf2–Lem3 in the E1, E1-ATP, E1P-ADP, E2P-transition, and E2P states, at resolutions of 2.8 Å to 4.0 Å (Figure 2—figure supplements 1–9, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM data processing and resolution assessment shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Cryo-EM 3D maps of Dnf2–Lem3 in E1, E1-ATP, E1P-ADP, E2P-transition, and E2P states were obtained at resolutions of 2.8 Å to 4.0 Å.
source: We obtained cryo-EM 3D maps of the S. cerevisiae Dnf1–Lem3 in the E1, E1P-ADP, and E2P states and Dnf2–Lem3 in the E1, E1-ATP, E1P-ADP, E2P-transition, and E2P states, at resolutions of 2.8 Å to 4.0 Å (Figure 2—figure supplements 1–9, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM data processing and resolution assessment shown in supplementary figures.

claim: The high-resolution 3D map at 2.8 Å of Dnf1–Lem3 in the E2P state enabled building the first atomic model of Dnf1–Lem3.
source: The high-resolution 3D map at 2.8 Å of the Dnf1–Lem3 in the E2P state enabled us to build the first atomic model of Dnf1–Lem3 (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the high-resolution cryo-EM map and the resulting atomic model.

claim: Almost the entire Dnf1–Lem3 complex is ordered and well resolved in the E2P state model.
source: Except for a few short and disordered loops, almost the entire complex is ordered and well resolved in this model.
evidence: This is based on the quality of the cryo-EM map and the completeness of the atomic model.

claim: Many extra densities were observed in the transmembrane region of Dnf1 in the E2P state.
source: Interestingly, many extra densities were observed in the transmembrane region of Dnf1 in the E2P state (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM density map shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Some extra densities in the transmembrane region belonged to the detergent CHS.
source: Some clearly belonged to the detergent CHS that was added during purification, while others located in the substrate-transport path resembled phospholipid, and they were so assigned, as will be described below.
evidence: This is based on the shape and location of the densities and knowledge of the purification conditions.

claim: Extra densities located in the substrate-transport path resembled phospholipid.
source: Some clearly belonged to the detergent CHS that was added during purification, while others located in the substrate-transport path resembled phospholipid, and they were so assigned, as will be described below.
evidence: This is based on the shape, size, and location of the densities in the cryo-EM map.

claim: Dnf1 has a 10-TMH transmembrane domain.
source: As expected of any P4 ATPase, Dnf1 has a 10-TMH TMD (TMH1-10)
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure and is consistent with known P4 ATPase architecture.

claim: Dnf1 has a cytosolic A domain inserted between TMH2 and TMH3.
source: a cytosolic A domain inserted between TMH2 and TMH3
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure.

claim: Dnf1 has cytosolic P and N domains inserted between TMH4 and TMH5.
source: and a cytosolic P domain and a cytosolic N domain, both inserted between TMH4 and TMH5 (Figure 2).
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure shown in Figure 2.

claim: The N-terminal peptide of Dnf1 preceding TMH1 is 204 residues long and is largely disordered except for the last 39-residue segment.
source: The amino terminal peptide preceding TMH1 (N-tail) of Dnf1 is 204 residues long and is largely disordered, except for the last 39-residue segment (Glu-166 to Leu-204), which is stabilized by binding to the regulatory A domain.
evidence: This is based on the cryo-EM density and the atomic model.

claim: The last 39-residue segment of the Dnf1 N-tail (Glu-166 to Leu-204) is stabilized by binding to the regulatory A domain.
source: The amino terminal peptide preceding TMH1 (N-tail) of Dnf1 is 204 residues long and is largely disordered, except for the last 39-residue segment (Glu-166 to Leu-204), which is stabilized by binding to the regulatory A domain.
evidence: This is observed in the structure where this segment has clear density and interacts with the A domain.

claim: The C-terminal peptide of Dnf1 following the 10th TMH is 157 residues long and is largely disordered except for the TMD-proximal 35-residue segment.
source: The carboxyl terminal peptide (C-tail) of Dnf1 following the 10th TMH is 157 residues long (Pro-1405 to Asn-1571) and is also largely disordered except for the TMD-proximal 35-residue segment (Pro-1405 to Lys-1439).
evidence: This is based on the cryo-EM density and the atomic model.

claim: The ordered Dnf1 C-tail segment contains a short α-helix equivalent to one that functions as a switch in Drs2.
source: Interestingly, this ordered Dnf1 C-tail segment contains a short α-helix, the equivalent of which was reported to function as a switch that converts the Drs2 flippase from its auto-inhibitory state to the active state in a unique PI4P-binding-dependent manner (Bai et al., 2019a).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison with Drs2 and cited literature.

claim: The Dnf1 C-tail helix is stabilized by the C-tail of Lem3 in a conformation corresponding to the active state of Drs2.
source: However, the Dnf1 helix is stabilized by the C-tail of Lem3 in a conformation corresponding to the active state of Drs2, suggesting that Dnf1 and Dnf2 do not require binding to a phosphoinositide at this site for activation.
evidence: This is based on structural observation and comparison with Drs2.

claim: Dnf1 and Dnf2 do not require binding to a phosphoinositide for activation.
source: However, the Dnf1 helix is stabilized by the C-tail of Lem3 in a conformation corresponding to the active state of Drs2, suggesting that Dnf1 and Dnf2 do not require binding to a phosphoinositide at this site for activation.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observation that the C-tail is already in an active conformation without PI4P binding.

claim: The Dnf1 C-tail interacts extensively with the cytoplasmic domains of Dnf1 in regulating the substrate-transport cycle.
source: The Dnf1 C-tail interacts extensively with the cytoplasmic domains of Dnf1 in regulating the substrate-transport cycle, as described below.
evidence: This is based on structural observations of interactions between the C-tail and cytoplasmic domains.

claim: Dnf1 and Dnf2 activity is regulated by two flippase kinases Fpk1 and Fpk2.
source: Dnf1 and Dnf2 activity is regulated by two flippase kinases Fpk1 and Fpk2.
evidence: This is established knowledge about regulation of these flippases.

claim: Mutations in Fpk1 and Fpk2 do not affect the subcellular location of Dnf1 and Dnf2.
source: Mutations in Fpk1 and Fpk2 do not affect the subcellular location of Dnf1 and Dnf2, but these enzymes have almost no activity in a fpk1,2∆ strain (Nakano et al., 2008; Roelants et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by cited functional studies.

claim: Dnf1 and Dnf2 have almost no activity in a fpk1,2∆ strain.
source: Mutations in Fpk1 and Fpk2 do not affect the subcellular location of Dnf1 and Dnf2, but these enzymes have almost no activity in a fpk1,2∆ strain (Nakano et al., 2008; Roelants et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by cited functional studies.

claim: All 17 known phosphorylation sites in Dnf1 are located in disordered loop regions.
source: We found that all 17 known phosphorylation sites (P32660 in the UniProt Database [UniProt Consortium, 2019]) are located in disordered loop regions in the Dnf1 structure: the N-tail, a loop between Thr-290 and Ala-378, and the C-tail.
evidence: This is based on mapping known phosphorylation sites onto the structure.

claim: PC flippases are autoinhibited and phosphorylation relieves the inhibition.
source: These observations suggest that the PC flippases are autoinhibited and phosphorylation, not PI4P binding as in the yeast PS flippases, relieves the inhibition.
evidence: This is inferred from the location of phosphorylation sites and comparison with PS flippases.

claim: Lem3 contains two TMHs flanking a large lumenal domain.
source: Similar to the yeast Cdc50 and human CDC50a, Lem3 contains two TMHs flanking a large lumenal domain.
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure and is consistent with other Cdc50 family members.

claim: The Lem3 TMHs are packed against the last TMH of Dnf1, TMH10.
source: These TMHs are packed against the last TMH of Dnf1, TMH10 (Figure 2).
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure shown in Figure 2.

claim: The Lem3 lumenal domain contains two disulfide bonds.
source: The Lem3 lumenal domain contains two disulfide bonds (Cys-110 with Cys-159 and Cys-216 with Cys-231)
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure.

claim: The Lem3 lumenal domain contains four N-glycans at Asn-240, Asn-256, Asn-298, and Asn-332.
source: and four N-glycans at Asn-240, Asn-256, Asn-298, and Asn-332.
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM density and modeled in the structure.

claim: Both the N-terminal and C-terminal regions of Lem3 are stable, in contrast to yeast Cdc50 and human CDC50a where these regions are disordered.
source: To our surprise, both the N-terminal and the C-terminal regions of Lem3 are stable, in contrast to the yeast Cdc50 and human CDC50a, in which these regions are disordered (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: This is based on comparison of the current structure with previously reported structures.

claim: The Lem3 N-terminal peptide preceding Asn-50 folds into a two-turn α-helix and binds the Dnf1 A domain.
source: The N-terminal peptide preceding Asn-50 folds into a two-turn α-helix and binds the Dnf1 A domain (Figure 2—figure supplement 11A–B).
evidence: This is observed in the structure shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: The exact sequence of the Lem3 N-tail α-helix was not resolved due to partial flexibility.
source: Due to a partial flexibility, the exact sequence of the Lem3 N-tail α-helix was not resolved.
evidence: This is based on the quality of the cryo-EM density in this region.

claim: The binding interface of the Lem3 N-tail in the A domain is highly positively charged.
source: However, we found its binding interface in the A domain is highly positively charged, featuring Lys-392, Lys-395, Arg-408, Arg-457, Lys-460, and Lys-516 (Figure 2—figure supplement 11C)
evidence: This is based on analysis of the electrostatic surface shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: The Lem3 N-tail segment between Glu-28 to Glu-42 is highly negative, containing 11 Asp and Glu residues.
source: and the Lem3 N-tail segment between Glu-28 to Glu-42 is highly negative, containing 11 Asp and Glu residues (Figure 2—figure supplement 11D).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: The short N-tail α-helix of Lem3 is most likely from the negatively charged region between Glu-28 to Glu-42.
source: Therefore, the short N-tail α-helix of Lem3p is most likely from this negatively charged region.
evidence: This is inferred from the electrostatic complementarity between the helix binding site and the negatively charged sequence region.

claim: The A domain moves significantly during the substrate-transport cycle of P4 ATPase.
source: Because the A domain moves significantly during the substrate-transport cycle of P4 ATPase, this unique, A domain-interacting, and highly negative Lem3 N-tail α-helix likely regulates lipid transport activity of Dnf1 and Dnf2, as described below.
evidence: This is based on comparison of structures in different states showing A domain movement.

claim: The unique, A domain-interacting, and highly negative Lem3 N-tail α-helix likely regulates lipid transport activity of Dnf1 and Dnf2.

evidence: This is based on structural superposition of different states.

claim: The lipid head group transports through the groove between TMH2 and TMH4, while lipid tails move on the hydrophobic surface of TM2 and TM4.
source: Combining the finding of two substrate-binding sites and the transport cycle, we propose that the lipid head group transports through the groove between TMH2 and TMH4, while lipid tails move accordingly on the hydrophobic surface of the TM2 and TM4.
evidence: This is a mechanistic proposal based on the structural findings.

claim: The proposed mechanism is essentially the same as the 'credit card model'.
source: This is essentially the same as the previously described 'credit card model' (Andersen et al., 2016; Roland and Graham, 2016).
evidence: This relates the current findings to a previously proposed model, supported by citations.

claim: The corresponding E1, E1-ATP, E1P-ADP, E1P, and E2P states of Dnf1/Dnf2 and ATP8A1–CDC50a are remarkably similar in domain architecture and substrate-transport path.
source: Aligning our structures in this paper with those of ATP8A1–CDC50a reveal that the corresponding E1, E1-ATP, E1P-ADP, E1P, and E2P states are remarkably similar in both domain architecture and substrate-transport path (Figure 6).
evidence: This is based on structural alignment shown in Figure 6.

claim: A common, conserved transport pathway exists regardless of the lipid substrate being flipped.
source: This results suggests a common, conserved transport pathway regardless of the lipid substrate being flipped.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural similarity between PC and PS flippases.

claim: Dnf1 and Dnf2 belong to the P4A class along with Drs2 and ATP8A1 in the phylogenetic classification.
source: In a recent phylogenetic classification, P4-ATPases are divided into P4A, P4B and P4C subclasses (Palmgren et al., 2019). In this scheme, Dnf1 and 2 belong to the same P4A class as Drs2 and ATP8A1.
evidence: This is based on a cited phylogenetic classification.

claim: The resemblance in structure and catalytic cycle between Dnf1/2 and Drs2/ATP8A1 supports the phylogenetic classification scheme.
source: The resemblance in structure and catalytic cycle between Dnf1/2 and Drs2/ATP8A1 supports this new classification scheme.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural similarities observed.

claim: Recent structural studies of human ATP11C–CDC50A flippase revealed a similar mechanism for lipid-flipping.
source: In further agreement with this scheme, recent structural studies of the human ATP11C–CDC50A flippase, also a P4A member in the new scheme, have revealed a rather similar mechanism for lipid-flipping (Nakanishi et al., 2020a; Nakanishi et al., 2020b).
evidence: This is supported by cited recent studies.

claim: All P4-ATPases may employ a similar substrate-transport mechanism.
source: While structural knowledge obtained thus far raises the possibility that all P4-ATPases employ a similar substrate-transport mechanism, more definitive support awaits further structure and functional analyses of P4-ATPases in the P4B and P4C classes.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on current structural knowledge, with acknowledgment that more data is needed.

claim: More definitive support for a universal P4-ATPase mechanism awaits further structure and functional analyses of P4B and P4C class members.
source: While structural knowledge obtained thus far raises the possibility that all P4-ATPases employ a similar substrate-transport mechanism, more definitive support awaits further structure and functional analyses of P4-ATPases in the P4B and P4C classes.
evidence: This acknowledges the limitation of current knowledge.

claim: In PS flippases Drs2 and ATP8A1, the C-terminal loop is auto-inhibitory and contains the conserved GF/YAFS motif.
source: In PS flippases such as the yeast Drs2 and human ATP8A1, the C-terminal loop is auto-inhibitory; this loop, which contains the conserved GF/YAFS motif, extends over and wraps around the cytoplasmic catalytic domains to stabilize these enzymes in the E2P state.
evidence: This is based on prior structural studies of PS flippases.

claim: The C-terminal loop of Dnf1 and Dnf2 doesn't contain the GF/YAFS motif and is disordered in the E2P state.
source: The C-terminal loop of Dnf1 and Dnf2 doesn't contain the GF/YAFS motif and is disordered in the E2P state.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and structural observation.

claim: There is a unique helix-turn-helix motif (E692-S737) in the N domain of Dnf1 and Dnf2 that is absent in Drs2 and ATP8A1.
source: However, there is a unique helix-turn-helix motif (E692-S737) in the N domain of Dnf1 and Dnf2 that is absent in Drs2 and ATP8A1 (Figure 6).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison shown in Figure 6.

claim: In the E1 state, the helix-turn-helix motif interacts with the P domain through Lys-702 and Arg-703 interacting with Glu-994, Asn-998, and Asn-1008.
source: In the E1 state, the helix-turn-helix interacts with the P domain, specifically, its Lys-702 and Arg-703 interacting with the P domain Glu-994, Asn-998, and Asn-1008.
evidence: This is directly observed in the E1 state structure.

claim: In the E1P-ADP state, the interaction of the helix-turn-helix with the P domain is weakened, with only Arg-703 interacting with Asn-998 and Asn-1008.
source: Upon ATP hydrolysis and enzyme phosphorylation in the E1P-ADP state, this interaction is weakened because only Arg-703 of the motif now interacts with the P domain Asn-998 and Asn-1008.
evidence: This is based on structural comparison between E1 and E1P-ADP states.

claim: In the E2P state, the helix-turn-helix motif shifts interaction from the P domain to the C-tail, with Glu-709 and Arg-713 forming electrostatic interactions with Arg-1434 and Lys-1436.
source: The release of ADP in the E2P state appears to shift the interaction of the Dnf1 and Dnf2 insertion from the P domain to the C-tail, with the helix-turn-helix Glu-709 and Arg-713 forming electrostatic interactions with the C-tail Arg-1434 and Lys-1436.
evidence: This is directly observed in the E2P state structure.

claim: The systematic changes in helix-turn-helix interactions suggest it may play a regulatory role in the substrate-transport cycle.
source: These systematic changes suggest that the Dnf1 and Dnf2 insertion may play a regulatory role in the substrate-transport cycle.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed state-dependent interactions.

claim: Deletion of the helix-turn-helix motif in Dnf1 strongly decreased transport of all substrates.
source: To examine this possibility, we deleted the motif in Dnf1 and performed an in vivo substrate uptake assay. The deletion strongly decreased transport of all substrates (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by lipid uptake assay data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The functional assay confirms a crucial role of the helix-turn-helix motif.
source: These results confirm a crucial role of the helix-turn-helix motif and reveal a unique aspect of the Dnf1/Dnf2 flippases over the otherwise conserved substrate-transport mechanism of the P4 ATPases.
evidence: This is concluded from the functional data.

claim: The helix-turn-helix motif reveals a unique aspect of Dnf1/Dnf2 flippases over the otherwise conserved substrate-transport mechanism of P4 ATPases.
source: These results confirm a crucial role of the helix-turn-helix motif and reveal a unique aspect of the Dnf1/Dnf2 flippases over the otherwise conserved substrate-transport mechanism of the P4 ATPases.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the structural and functional data.

claim: The overall substrate-transport mechanism is similar between PC and PS flippases and may be conserved among all classes of P4 ATPases.
source: In summary, our systematic structural and biochemical studies of the Dnf1–Lem3 and Dnf2–Lem3 complexes in five transport states provide the novel insight that the overall substrate-transport mechanism is similar to that of PS flippases and that it may be conserved among all classes of the P4 ATPases.
evidence: This is a major conclusion of the study based on structural and functional comparisons.

claim: The helix-turn-helix motif in the P domain is unique to class-3 enzymes and plays a crucial regulatory function during the substrate-transport cycle.
source: Our studies also show a helix-turn-helix motif in the P domain that is unique to the class-3 enzymes and plays a crucial regulatory function during the substrate-transport cycle.
evidence: This is a major finding supported by structural and functional data.

claim: The role of the beta-subunit Lem3 in substrate binding and specificity is unique to class-3 enzymes.
source: Also unique to class-3 enzymes is the role of the beta-subunit Lem3 in substrate binding and specificity.
evidence: This is a major finding supported by structural and functional data.

claim: This work advances mechanistic understanding of the highly conserved and essential family of P4 ATPases.
source: Thus, this work advances our mechanistic understanding of the highly conserved and essential family of the P4 ATPases.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the study's contribution.

source: This comparison suggests that Dnf1 and Dnf2 have highly similar structures and go through virtually the same functional states during their respective substrate-transport cycles. This finding was not surprising, because these two flippases share a high sequence identity of about 69%
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison.

source: By comparing the 3D maps of Dnf1–Lem3 and Dnf2–Lem3 in the E1, E1P-ADP, and E2P states, which were the three states observed for both flippases, we found that the structures were superimposable in all three states (Figure 2—figure supplement 10).
